activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
story:
The family group chat, named "Vitale Family Headquarters" by his mother in a moment she now regretted, lit up at 7:14 on Thursday evening. Matteo sat at the kitchen counter with his phone in one hand and his dance permission slip in the other, watching the messages stack like dominoes. Grandma had sent three thumbs-up emojis. His aunt had asked whether there would be adult supervision. Then his mother typed: "Matteo, do you actually know how to dance? Asking for a friend."

He put the phone face down on the counter. That was the problem, and the group chat knew it before he did. At the last family wedding, two years ago, he had done a move he still thought of as "the fallen tree," and his cousin had posted the video, which had caused a small controversy at school until Mohamad argued that making fun of it was basically bullying. Mohamad had nominated the fallen tree as "iconic," which was kind, and also not the same as dancing well.

The dance was tomorrow night. Lara had already texted him a checklist of songs she hoped the DJ would play, and Mohamad had claimed he would just stand near the speakers and nod. Standing near the speakers and nodding was a strategy, Matteo supposed, but not one he wanted to copy.

He picked the phone back up, mostly to change the subject, and scrolled. His aunt had moved on to Mr. Joseph, the neighbour, whose cockatoo, Snowball, had apparently been on television. "That bird is a better dancer than any of us," she wrote, with a video attached.

Matteo pressed play. Snowball was white with a yellow crest, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, and he was bouncing and stepping and swinging his head while a pop song played. His mother had forwarded an article too, one from 2009, about scientists led by a man named Aniruddh Patel. They had shown that Snowball could move in time to the music, and when the researchers changed the tempo, slowed it down or sped it up, Snowball adjusted. The bird wasn't copying somebody off camera, the article said, because they had checked that.

Matteo read the paragraph twice. A bird. Keeping the beat. Adjusting when the tempo changed. He thought about the fallen tree and about how he had never once, at that wedding, tried to find the beat. He had just waved his arms and hoped.

He typed into the group chat: "Tomorrow at the dance I'm going to do what the cockatoo does. Just find the beat and step with it. If it works for him, it can work for me."

His mother replied within a minute. "It would be negligent of me not to mention that you are not, in fact, a bird."

"Grandma's right, though," his aunt wrote. "Snowball's better than all of us."

Matteo set down the phone, put on the song from the video, and practised stepping in time, once, twice, twenty times, while his mother watched from the doorway and did not laugh.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion, so not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing.
story:
The bus wouldn't reach school for another twelve minutes, and Mr. Dang's quiz on "The Lighthouse Keeper" was first period. Joseph had the story open on his lap, its cover bent back, while Iris leaned over the seat in front of him.

"It's obviously the brother," Iris said, tapping the page. "Paragraph three mentions he keeps a knife in his sock drawer. That's foreshadowing. He did it."

Eli nodded from across the aisle. "And the keeper's dog growls whenever the brother shows up. That's symbolism. Dogs sense evil."

Joseph ran his thumb down the margin. Twelve minutes. He counted the times the brother appeared before the theft: seven mentions, and every single one pointed at him like an arrow. It felt too easy. "Why would the author tell us everything by page two?" he asked.

"Because it's foreshadowing," Iris said. "Mr. Dang said foreshadowing hints at what's coming."

"That's the thing." Joseph flipped back to paragraph three. "There's a rule in mysteries. A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion. Not every hint is real foreshadowing." He looked up. "The knife, the growling dog, all of it could be bait."

Eli frowned. "You're saying the author is messing with us?"

"I'm saying we should test it." Joseph searched the last page again, the one where the keeper discovers the lamp missing. If the brother stole it, there'd be something about the sock drawer being empty, or the dog going quiet. Nothing. What there was, instead, was one line he'd skimmed past: the keeper's own hygiene kit, with its bottle of lamp oil, packed for his trip. The keeper had stolen his own lamp to collect the insurance money, and the kit was the real clue, sitting in plain sight.

"He did it himself," Joseph said. "The brother's a red herring. All seven mentions, a dead end on purpose."

"Prove it," Iris said.

"Page nine. The oil in his kit. The theft happened the night before his trip. And the dog growls at everybody, even the postman, page five."

The bus swung onto Maple. Eight minutes left. Iris pulled out her notebook and wrote fast, her pen skipping. "So for the quiz, we say the knife is a false clue, the dog is a distraction, and the hygiene kit is the real foreshadowing?"

"And symbolism," Joseph said. "The lighthouse going dark. That's the fundamental thing about the whole story. He's supposed to be the one guiding people, and he's the one who snuffs the light out."

Eli grinned. "Mr. Dang is going to lose it when we say the brother is innocent."

"We could be wrong," Iris said.

"We could," Joseph agreed. "But if I set a trap for readers, that's exactly how I'd build it."

The bus hissed to a stop in front of the school. Iris snapped her notebook shut, and the three of them filed down the steps, Joseph still holding the story open to page nine, his finger keeping the place.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Thailand, the head is considered sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude.
story:
Alexandre had been sent next door with a jar of his mother's jam, because the new neighbours had moved in on Tuesday and his mother believed in welcome gifts. The house smelled of lemongrass and something frying. A woman opened the door, pressed her palms together, and bowed slightly, so Alexandre put the jar in one hand and tried the same gesture back. Her smile widened, and she called something over her shoulder. A boy about seven appeared, and behind him came an older girl Alexandre recognized from school, Maddison, from Mr. Lawrence's homeroom, though he had never spoken to her.

"You brought a gift," Maddison said. "That's good. Come in, take off your shoes." She pointed at a rack of sandals by the door, and Alexandre worked his sneakers off while balancing the jar. In the kitchen the table was already being set, and he watched the woman scoop rice into a pot with a flat basket, measuring with her finger. Maddison explained the ratio to him: one knuckle of water above the rice, no more. Her aunt, she said, could do it without measuring at all.

The little boy was showing Alexandre a plastic ant farm he had built in a shoebox, where six ants were trying to colonize the corner near the apple slice. Alexandre crouched to look, and the boy leaned in beside him, grinning, his hair sticking up in tufts. Without thinking, Alexandre reached over and ruffled it. The boy went still. The aunt stopped mid-motion at the stove. Maddison's mouth tightened.

"Sorry," she said quickly, pulling Alexandre toward the window. "In Thailand the head is sacred. Touching someone's head is rude, even if you're just being nice to a kid." The boy had backed away and was rubbing his hair flat, watching Alexandre with wide eyes but no tears. Through the translucent curtain over the sink, Alexandre could see his own front porch, and he thought about how many times he had seen his uncle pat kids on the head at family picnics. Different houses, different rules. There had to be a way to fix it.

At dinner he tried everything the way they did it: spoon in the right hand, fork in the left, no elbows, no reaching. When the little boy passed him the chili sauce without being asked, Alexandre remembered the jar of jam sitting on the counter, still wrapped in its ribbon. He asked Maddison to translate, then told the boy the jam was for him, from Alexandre's house, and that next time he would bring the good kind with the whole strawberries. The boy looked at his aunt, who nodded, and then he carried the jar to the shelf beside the ant farm and set it where he could see it from the table.

"Strawberries," he said in English, carefully, tasting the word.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In a fair test, everything except the variable being tested is kept the same, such as the amount, the temperature and the timing.
story:
Parker's best paper airplane, the Silver Dart, had flown clear across the gym on Friday. On Saturday it nose-dived into the birdbath after four meters. Something was wrong, and he meant to find out.

"Maybe you built it badly," said Cayson, who had come over to accompany him to the park and had stayed to watch the crash.

"I built one plane, one time," Parker said. "Same folds, same paper." He fetched the Dart from the wet grass, dried it on his shirt, and threw it again. It wobbled and dropped. In the gym it had sailed. Same plane, two different results. Something invisible had to be changing it.

Aanya climbed over the back fence, as she always did on Saturdays. "What are you doing?"

"Testing a guess," Parker said. "My hypothesis is that the plane itself is fine, and something outside is ruining the flights."

"That's a big word for a guess," said Aanya.

"A testable guess," Parker said. "That's the whole point. I can check it."

Aanya squinted up at the maple tree, where the top leaves were moving. "It's windy," she said.

"But the gym has no wind," said Cayson. "So of course it flew better inside."

"Then throw both," Aanya said. She ran home and returned with a second sheet of the exact same paper from the same ream Parker had used, and Parker folded a second Dart, matching every crease. "Two planes," she said, "same amount of paper, same design. Now change only one thing."

Parker was hesitant at first, because the plan seemed too simple to prove anything. But he threw the first plane from the patio into the open yard, where the wind caught it and flipped it sideways into the hedge. Then, holding the second plane exactly the same way, he stepped through the sliding door and launched it down the hallway. It glided past the coats and landed softly at the far wall.

"Same paper, same folds, same throw, same time of day," Parker said, counting on his fingers. "The only thing different was the wind. So the wind did it. The plane isn't bad."

"That's the insight that matters," Aanya said. "If you'd changed two things at once, like using different paper outside and the same paper inside, you'd never know which one caused the flop."

Parker grinned and carried both planes back to the patio. He wanted one more throw, and this time he waited for the gusts to stop, counted five, and launched the Silver Dart high into the still air between breezes. It rode a sudden updraft, sailed over the fence, and landed in Ms. Rossi's garden, right on top of her freshly planted seedlings.

"Nice calm-air test," Cayson called after him as Parker climbed the fence to retrieve it. Ms. Rossi was already standing there, holding the plane and a watering can.

"Indoor or outdoor?" she asked.

"Outdoor," Parker admitted.

"Figures," said Ms. Rossi. "This is the only paper airplane that's ever landed in my garden, and it's the one that flew well."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Scientists assign people to groups at random so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly, rather than letting people choose their group.
story:
The group chat pinged at 9:04, right after Romy had closed her science book. Winnie: "HELP. my mom's cousin was in that new headache medicine study and she got better!! so the medicine works, right??" Romy stared at the screen. She wanted to say yes, because Winnie had been trying all week to find a topic for her science fair project about medicine, and this sounded like a gift. But something about it itched.

Romy: "one person getting better is a story tho. not proof." Winnie replied with a single angry face, and Arizona jumped in: "romy's right but also rude." Romy chewed her lip. She remembered last fall, when her grandmother had sworn that honey dissolved in tea cured her sore throat in a day. Romy had gotten a sore throat two weeks later, drank plain water, and felt better in a day too. One person's experience, she had learned then, couldn't tell you what caused what. Her skepticism had started there, in her grandmother's kitchen, and it had never quite gone away.

Arizona: "ok but if the medicine doesn't work how do they even test it??" Romy didn't know, exactly, and that bothered her more than the headache question. She typed: "brb," grabbed her laptop, and searched the study her mom had mentioned once. Twenty minutes later she was back, screenshot pasted into the chat. Romy: "FOUND IT. the scientists didn't let anyone choose. they assigned people to the medicine group or the sugar-pill group at random, like a coin flip."

Winnie: "why?? choosing sounds nicer." Romy's fingers hovered. She read the line on her screen again, wanting to get it right. Romy: "so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly between the groups instead of all piling up in one." Arizona: "ohhh. like if you let people pick, maybe all the healthiest people pick the real medicine and then it LOOKS like the medicine works great." Winnie sent three brain emojis. Romy grinned at her phone.

Winnie: "ok but wait. my mom's cousin still got better." Romy: "she got better. we just can't tell WHY from her alone. that's the whole difference." There was a long pause, three dots appearing and dissolving, and then Winnie sent: "new idea. my science fair project = i test whether study volunteers who pick their own groups end up different from randomly assigned ones. i can use the class. can i borrow your notes??"

Romy: "yes. one condition. i get to hold the coin."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number, so each element has one more proton than the element before it.
story:
The giant periodic table poster hung above the whiteboard, and Zachary had never once looked at it until the day Ms. Choi announced a quiz. "Friday," she said. "You'll need to find the number of protons in any element I give you." Zachary's stomach dropped. He could barely find oxygen on that wall of squares.

That night he stared at his battered textbook, its resilient cover still holding together after three years of abuse. He thought back to September, when he'd sat in this same classroom feeling confident, and Ms. Choi had called on him first. "Zachary, what does the number in each box mean?" He'd shrugged, and Braeden had whispered "atomic number" just loudly enough to save him. He hadn't asked what an atomic number actually was. That was the mistake he kept repeating: getting the word without getting the thing.

At lunch on Thursday, Abbie dragged him to the science room and pointed at the poster. "Look at the top corner. Hydrogen, one. Then helium, two. Lithium, three." She ran her finger across the row, and Zachary noticed something he'd missed all year. The numbers counted upward, one at a time, in order, from left to right and down through the whole table. "They go up by one every single square," he said slowly. "So each element has one more proton than the element before it." Nobody had told him that. He'd seen it.

He had to be sure. He retrieved his pencil from his bag and wrote a test for himself, because a pattern you haven't tested is just a guess. "If silver is forty-seven," he said, "then the one right after it, cadmium, should be forty-eight. Forty-eight protons." Abbie checked the boxes. Forty-seven, then forty-eight. He picked a harder pair from a category he'd never touched, the metals near the bottom, and counted forward through five elements in a row. Each number was exactly one higher than the last. His rule held.

On Friday, Ms. Choi slid the quiz onto his desk. The third question read: "An element sits directly after nitrogen in the periodic table. Nitrogen's atomic number is seven. How many protons does the element after it have?" Zachary smiled. One more than seven. He wrote "eight," set down his pencil, and glanced up at the poster on the wall. "You could've just told us," he whispered to it, and Braeden, two seats over, snickered.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light.
story:
The lights went out all at once, and the farmhouse kitchen dropped into blue evening shadow. Emily's flashlight rolled across the counter where she'd left it, and she grabbed it before her little brother could accuse her of hogging it again. "Power cut," her mom called from the pantry, sounding almost cheerful. "Candles on the porch table. Nobody open the fridge."

The real problem arrived ten minutes later. Emily had a biology worksheet due tomorrow, a diagram of a frog's digestive tract she was supposed to label, and the word "intestine" sitting blank and smug on the page. By candlelight the diagram's fine lines vanished into shadow. She squinted, turned the paper at angles, and finally gave up and carried it outside, where her brother was already lying flat on the porch steps like a starfish.

He wasn't starfishing for nothing. The sky above the dark farmhouse was crowded with stars, more than Emily had ever counted from the yard, and a pale hazy band stretched right across it like spilled sugar. "What's that smudge?" her brother asked. "Is it a cloud?"

Emily wondered too. She got her phone and pulled up the page she'd found for a school project last month, the one she'd almost deleted. Before her battery died, the screen showed the line she remembered: a 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light. She read it out loud, twice, so it would stick.

"The Milky Way," her brother said. "That's the smudge?"

"That's the smudge." Emily didn't just want to believe the website, though. She had an idea she could actually test. "Okay, think about it. When the power's on, the porch light glows, the barn light glows, and the whole sky looks washed out. Watch this." She walked to the porch light switch and clicked it up and down uselessly, then held her flashlight toward the sky instead and clicked that on and off, on and off, while her brother stared upward. "See how the stars near the beam go faint? Now imagine a whole town of beams."

"So the power cut is like the flashlight off?" her brother said slowly. "For everybody?"

"Maybe for miles." She turned the flashlight off and the dark rushed back in, deeper than before, and the sugar-spill band seemed to thicken. Mr. Boateng, their neighbour from down the road, was walking past the fence with his own candle lantern, and he stopped to look up. "Haven't seen this sky since I was a boy," he said.

Her brother started a spontaneous game of connect-the-dots, inventing a constellation shaped like a wolverine, and Emily sat down next to him with her worksheet on her knee, tracing the frog's intestine by starlight. Somewhere down the valley the transformer hummed, then snapped back on, and every window in the farmhouse lit up yellow.

The stars didn't vanish all at once. They faded, one slow handful at a time, like they were being poured back into a jar.

"Do it again," her brother whispered.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: After flying across time zones, the body clock adjusts at an average of about one day for each hour of time difference.
story:
Wyatt had been staring at the ceiling of the cabin for an hour when the clock on the nightstand flipped to 12:14. Outside, the national park was pure black, and somewhere in that blackness a river muttered over its rocks. His parents were asleep in the next room, his little sister too, and here he was, wide awake, as if it were the middle of the afternoon. Two nights ago they had flown west across six time zones for this trip, and on the first night he had blamed the excitement. Tonight he wondered if something else was going on.

He got up quietly and sat by the window. He tried to categorize what he knew, the way he did for science class. Fact one: at home it would be six hours later right now, so his body probably thought it was early evening. Fact two: last night he had been wide awake at midnight too. Fact three: his dad had fallen asleep at dinner and woken at five in the morning, ravenous. There was a pattern, and patterns meant rules.

At the visitor center the next morning, Wyatt found Shay and Israel from the junior ranger program poking at the earthquake display. He told them his theory. "I think your body stays on home time," he said, "and it fixes itself slowly. Like it takes a certain number of days per hour of time difference."

"A percentage of an hour?" Israel said. "Like half a day per hour?"

"More than that," Wyatt said. "I was awake at midnight on night two, six hours off. If I'm still a little off on day six, that works out to about one day for each hour of difference." He shrugged. "That's my guess, anyway."

The plan they came up with was simple: test it. Wyatt would stop napping, get sunlight in the morning, and each night he would write down how awake he felt at midnight, from one to ten. Ms. Rosen, the ranger leading their group, saw the notebook and asked what the columns were for. "A jet lag experiment," Wyatt said. She smiled and said only, "Six hours is a big jump," which was no help at all, and he liked that.

The experiment ran all week. Day three: awake at eleven, sleepy by one. Day four: asleep by midnight, awake too early. Day five: he slept until almost eight, later than at home. Day six, at the campfire program near the lodge where all the affluent tour groups stayed in their fancy cabins, Wyatt caught himself yawning at nine and being out cold before his head fully hit the pillow. Six days, six hours, almost exactly one day per hour. He found Shay by the fire and showed her the notebook, and she laughed and said, "Congratulations, your body is finally in this time zone." He grinned, and then stopped grinning, because it was the last night of the trip.

Tomorrow they would fly home, back across the same six hours, and the whole clock would be wrong again. He would be wide awake at midnight in his own bed, missing a river he could hear from a cabin he would never see again, waiting for a body that fixed itself exactly one day for each hour and never any faster. He zipped the notebook into his backpack and went to say goodnight to Israel, who was still up, scribbling by flashlight.

"How many days until your body's back on home time?" Israel asked.

"Six," Wyatt said. "Maybe five, if I'm lucky."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2, which makes it strongly acidic compared with most things people drink.
story:
Savannah lined up seven cups on the kitchen counter like a tiny army waiting for inspection. Each cup held a mystery liquid: milk, soapy water, lemon juice, soda, vinegar, baking soda mixed with water, and one containing only tap water, which Finnley insisted on calling "the control group" even though they had both learned that phrase only yesterday.

"Bet you a cookie lemon juice is neutral," Finnley said, leaning on the counter with an air of great confidence. "It's food. Food is normal. Normal stuff is neutral. That's just science."

"That is not science," Savannah said. "That is you guessing and then acting proud about it." She tore open the little packet of litmus paper she had acquired from Ms. Njoroge after class, along with a photocopied pH chart that smelled like the copy machine. The chart ran from zero to fourteen, red on one end, blue on the other, with seven sitting in the middle like a referee.

They started with the soap. Finnley dunked a strip and it turned blue, which meant basic, and he did a small trumpet fanfare with his mouth. The baking soda water went blue too. The vinegar strip turned a fierce pink, and the soda a softer one, and the milk barely blushed at all.

Then the lemon juice. Savannah dipped the strip and held it against the chart, and the paper went so red it looked embarrassed. It matched the color sitting next to the number two.

"Two," she said slowly, following the chart down. "The whole scale goes to fourteen, and lemon juice is at two."

Finnley leaned in, squinting with the acute focus of someone losing a cookie. "That's way over on the acid side. That's more acidic than the vinegar strip."

"The vinegar's around three. Lemon juice is more acidic than that. It's strongly acidic compared with most stuff people drink." Savannah turned the strip in the light. "People put that on pancakes."

"You owe me nothing," Finnley said, "because I was wrong, and I accept my fate with dignity." He slid the cookie plate across the counter to her anyway. "I changed my mind about lemon juice, obviously. Food can absolutely be acid. My whole worldview is different now."

"It's juice, not a plot twist."

"Everything's a plot twist when you have test strips." Finnley picked up the lemon itself, the actual lemon, and examined it like a detective. "This little guy seems so innocent. Like, what if it's secretly a carnivore? What if lemons hunt?"

"They don't hunt. They just sit there being sour."

Savannah bit the cookie, wrote "lemon juice, pH 2" in her notebook, and drew a small angry face next to it. Then she held up the last strip over the cup of tap water. "Final test. Neutral, right?"

Finnley raised one hand like he was swearing an oath. "If that paper turns any color at all, I'm moving to another planet."

Savannah dropped the strip in and they both leaned over the cup, noses almost touching the rim, watching it float.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The Rubin vase, introduced by Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915, can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.
story:
The poster contest at the community centre had one rule: the picture had to make people look twice. Audrey had spent all week on her entry, a black-and-white drawing she'd found in Mr. Delgado's old psychology book when she was killing time in the reading room. She wanted the blue ribbon that hung every year above the front desk, and more than that, she wanted to beat Zackery, who had won the last two contests in a row.

She pinned her poster to the corkboard near the vending machines and stepped back. Zackery came down the hall with Callan, both of them carrying swim bags, Zackery still flexing a hand he'd jammed a tendon in during practice, his wrist wrapped in white tape. He stopped in front of her poster and frowned.

"Two faces," he said, pointing. "That's what it is. Two people about to kiss or argue or something."

"Are you blind?" Callan pushed in beside him. "It's a vase. A white vase on a black background. That's obviously a vase." They argued all the way to the sign-in table, where Mr. Delgado was stapling the contest numbers to the wall. Audrey followed them, feeling odd, because she had drawn neither thing on purpose. She had copied the shape exactly, and until that moment she had seen only the vase.

"It's called a Rubin vase," Mr. Delgado said mildly, without looking up from his stapler. He tapped the psychology book sticking out of her tote bag. "Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin, 1915. You can see it as a vase or as two faces, but never both at the same moment." Then he went back to his numbers, as if he hadn't just said the most frustrating thing Audrey had heard all day.

Never both at the same moment. On the walk home through the arid, dusty lot behind the centre, where the grass had gone brown from the heat, she tested it. She stared at the poster image in her mind and tried to hold vase and faces together. She blinked fast. She crossed her eyes. She squinted at the chain-link fence and tried to stack the shapes over the diamonds. Nothing worked. The picture flipped, vase to faces, faces to vase, like a light switch, and she could catch herself in the middle of the flip but never in both. She tried to classify what was happening: the drawing itself never changed, so the flipping had to happen somewhere she couldn't see, somewhere behind her eyes. That was the part that kept her up that night, the idea that two people could stand in front of the exact same thing and both be completely right.

On judging day, the room was crowded. Callan had taped a paper sign under her poster that said THE VASE in block letters. Zackery, whose own entry was a slick photo of a basketball hoop, tore the sign down when he thought nobody was looking, but Audrey saw, and Callan saw her see it. Zackery wanted his interpretation to win, wanted to be the one who named things first, the way he always had. Audrey watched him ball up Callan's sign and hold it behind his back, and she watched him look at Callan's face, and she watched him flatten the paper out again and smooth it against his knee.

The judge, a woman from the library, stood in front of Audrey's poster for a long time. "It keeps changing on me," she said, half laughing. She wrote something on her clipboard, then leaned toward Mr. Delgado and asked him a question Audrey couldn't hear. When the ribbons went up, the blue one hung over Zackery's basketball hoop. Audrey got red, second place, and a small note card from the judge: "Best conversation starter." Callan got nothing at all. Audrey found him outside by the bike racks, and she held up her note card so he could read it. He shrugged, still staring at the pavement, but then he said, "Tomorrow I'm bringing a marker. I'm writing THE VASE and THE FACES under it, both, with an arrow in the middle." Zackery came out the door with his blue ribbon in his fist, stopped, and said, "You'll need two arrows." Audrey pulled the cap off Callan's marker for him.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In Richard Connell's 1924 story The Most Dangerous Game, the island's name, Ship-Trap Island, and sailors' fear of it hint at the danger waiting there.
story:
The school library smelled like glue and old paper because the district had sent workers to renovate the back corner, and half the shelves sat pushed together under plastic sheets. Connor spread his copy of "The Most Dangerous Game" on the only clear table, next to a worksheet with two questions on it. "Find one example of foreshadowing," the worksheet said, "and explain what it suggests." He read the question three times, and it still looked like the teacher had written it in a language he'd never studied.

Pyper dropped into the chair across from him with a thump. "You got Mr. Kerr's sheet too?" she asked. "I picked the riddle story. The one with the umbrella in the first paragraph." She flipped her book open like it was easy, which made Connor's stomach knot.

"I picked the island one," Connor said. "There's this guy Rainsford, on a yacht, and he falls overboard." He ran his finger down the first page, hunting for anything that might count. Then a word snagged him, the way a hook snags a sleeve. "Wait. Listen to this. At the start, the sailors say the place gives them a shivering feeling of dread. The island's called Ship-Trap Island."

"So?"

"So why would an author name an island Ship-Trap Island? Nobody names a place after a thing that never happens there." Connor tapped the page. "Sailors are scared of it too, before anything's gone wrong. That's not just a name. That's the story whispering something bad is waiting on that island." He sat back, feeling something click into place, the way a jammed locker finally pops. "Is that foreshadowing? The name hinting at danger?"

"Write it down before you lose it," Pyper said. "I found a sticky note in my locker this morning, by the way." She slid a torn yellow square across the table. "Clement left it."

The note read: "Connor. Do NOT pick the island story. Everyone picks the island story. Signed, Clement." Under that, in smaller letters: "P.S. If you already picked it, look at the very first page. Trust me."

Connor laughed out loud, loud enough that Mr. Kerr glanced over from the returns desk and raised one finger to his lips. Connor lowered his voice. "He knew. Clement figured it out before I did." It was annoying and also, somehow, encouraging. If Clement could find it, the trick wasn't magic. It was a habit, like checking the weather before a hike.

He filled in his answer in careful pencil: The island's name, Ship-Trap Island, and the sailors' fear of it suggest the danger waiting there before Rainsford even arrives. Then he thought about the second question, symbolism, and frowned again. Pyper leaned over. "For mine, the umbrella stands for something. Like how the character pretends everything's tranquil when it isn't." She drew a little calm lake in the margin. "Fake peacefulness. That's my symbol."

Connor looked back at his story, where the yacht's lights were calm and the sea looked tranquil right up until Rainsford fell. "So the peaceful water might be the disguise," he said slowly. "The story keeps saying everything's fine, and fine is a lie." He started writing again, and this time the pencil moved without stopping. When the bell rang, he carried his sheet to Mr. Kerr's desk, and Mr. Kerr read it, and looked up.

"Ship-Trap Island," Mr. Kerr said, and slid the paper back with a small nod. "You found the trap."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: The Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today, was developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany.
story:
The back seat of the van smelled like sunscreen and old raisins, and Aurora had both climate graphs taped to the window so the highway light made the paper glow. One graph was from a rainforest station, one from a desert station, and both were due in Ms. Goh's class on Monday, which was a problem, because Monday was two thousand kilometres away in the wrong direction. "Look at this," she said, poking Tony's shoulder. "The rainforest gets more rain in its driest month than the desert gets all year." Tony squinted at the bars. "So the desert is basically the rainforest's evil twin." Joaquin, whose family shared the trip, leaned over from the middle seat. "That's not science, that's a movie trailer."

Aurora had started the project confident, and that was the humiliation she kept replaying. On Thursday she had stood at the whiteboard, pointed at the desert graph, and announced that its temperature line proved the desert was hotter than the rainforest every single month. Ms. Goh had said nothing, only raised an eyebrow and tapped the rainforest graph, where the temperature line sat stubbornly high and flat all year. Aurora had argued for a full minute before the class realized the rainforest was actually warmer on average, and Dev had snickered, and she had sat down with her ears on fire. In the parking lot afterward, Tony had tried to console her with half a granola bar and the words, "At least you were loudly wrong instead of quietly wrong," which somehow helped.

Now she flipped the graphs over, where she'd copied the little climate map from the atlas. Each region had a strange code stamped on it. The rainforest was marked Af. The desert was BWh. "What do these even mean?" she muttered. Joaquin grabbed the atlas and riffled through the front pages until he found a paragraph about the codes. "They're from the Koppen climate classification," he read. "It says it's still used on climate maps today." Aurora took the book. The paragraph said it was developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany.

"So a guy born in Russia, working in Germany, invented the codes that Ms. Goh's map is covered in," Aurora said slowly. "And nobody told us, because it's just sitting in the front of the atlas like it's boring." Tony leaned between the seats. "Koppen probably never drove through a desert in a van with a broken air conditioner. He just sat in Germany labeling the entire planet." Joaquin said, "That's honestly the most confident thing anyone has ever done with letters."

Aurora smoothed the graphs flat on her knees. The codes were crucial now, because if Af and BWh meant something real, she could check her comparison against them instead of guessing. She noticed the W in BWh and the f in Af, and she had a small test: she circled every code on the map that contained the same letters and counted how many dry regions shared the B. "Dry climates all get the B," she said. "Wet forest ones get the f. I'm going to test it on the mountain station when we stop." Tony said, "You're doing homework on vacation," and she said, "I'm doing revenge on a whiteboard." At the next rest stop, while their parents argued about the map, she laid the atlas across the picnic table and ran her finger down the legend, hunting for a B she couldn't explain.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Desert rainfall is not just low but unreliable: a desert may go years with almost no rain and then get a heavy downpour in a single storm.
story:
"Isabella, why does a desert have flood warning signs?" Nicola asked from the back seat, waving her phone at the screen. "That's like putting a shark sign in a cornfield."

They were three hours into the drive to Aunt Rosa's house, and Isabella had a folder on her lap with two printed graphs for her science homework. One showed rainfall for a rainforest, with tall bars stacked evenly month after month. The other, for a desert, was almost flat. "Because whoever put them there is bad at geography," she said. But the signs kept coming, leaning out of the gravel like they knew something she didn't.

"Your graphs might explain it," Nicola said, squinting over her shoulder. Ms. Ngo, their neighbor, had offered to drive them and was apparently also offering homework help, which was not the deal. "Work it out yourselves," Ms. Ngo said, keeping her eyes on the road. "That's the fun part." Isabella groaned, but she looked anyway. The desert graph was flat and boring until one single bar shot up like a skyscraper among garden fences. One storm, more rain than the whole rest of the year put together. She traced it with her finger. "Wait. It's not just that deserts get less rain. It's that you can't count on it. Years can go by with almost nothing, and then one storm dumps everything at once."

"So the ground is like..." Nicola rummaged in her snack bag, "like beef jerky. Hard, dry, can't soak anything up fast."

"Exactly. So a big downpour just runs off." Isabella felt the idea click into place, elastic, stretching to cover the weird road signs and the dry ditches and even the strange concrete channels beside the highway. She scribbled a note comparing the two graphs: rainforest, reliable and steady; desert, low and unpredictable. "Ms. Ngo, is that it? Is that why the signs are there?"

Ms. Ngo smiled at the windshield. "You tell me."

Over dinner at a diner with a sagging elastic band around the menus, Isabella spread the graphs between the ketchup and the salt. "We should form an alliance," she told Nicola. "You draw the posters for my presentation, I'll do the talking." Nicola agreed, mostly because Isabella had promised to nurture her newfound obsession with desert lizards by including a whole slide on them, which had nothing to do with rainfall and everything to do with friendship.

When they got back in the car, rain began to fall, gentle and steady. Isabella watched the drops streak the window and thought of the desert, waiting years for its one wild storm. "First one to spot a flash flood sign wins," she said. Nicola was already looking.

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: Rice seedlings are often grown first in a small nursery bed and then transplanted, often by hand, into flooded paddy fields.
story:
Eleanor spread her notecards across her grandmother's kitchen table, which smelled of cardamom and old newspapers. Ms. Menon had assigned her the monsoon for Monday's presentation, and so far her notes said only that it rains a lot in summer in South Asia, which even Edmund could have guessed.

"You are frowning at the table," her grandmother said, setting down two glasses of milk.

"I have to explain why the monsoon happens. Not just that it happens. And I can't see air, so how am I supposed to explain something invisible?"

Her grandmother sat down slowly, pressing one knuckle against her hip the way she did in damp weather. "Then make the air visible."

Eleanor thought about that while the kettle heated. When it whistled, she held a cold dinner plate above the spout and watched the steam curl upward, fog the glass, and drip back down as water. "So the land heats up in summer," she said, turning the plate in her hands, "the air over it rises like this steam, and wet air from the ocean moves in to take its place. That air rises too, cools, and the water falls as rain." It was a hidden cause, a pattern she couldn't watch in the sky, but she could watch it in her grandmother's kitchen.

"That is the shape of it," her grandmother said. "Now say why the rain matters."

"Because of rice?" Eleanor guessed. "Rice needs a lot of water."

"More than you think. Your grandfather and I, we grew rice. The seedlings begin in a small nursery bed, crowded together like sleeping babies, and then we pulled them up and transplanted them into the flooded paddy fields, one handful at a time, all of it done by hand." She flexed her fingers on the table. "Thousands of seedlings, bent double all day. The monsoon fills those paddies, so we waited for it, and when it came, everyone in the village moved."

Eleanor wrote it down, then stopped writing. She had been dreading the assignment all week, and now she wanted it to last longer. "Your hands hurt because of the rice."

"Because of the rice, yes. And because of the rice, we ate, and you exist." Her grandmother laughed, but the laugh had a rough edge. "A revolution of weather every year. The whole year turns around that rain, and my whole life has turned around it too."

That evening Eleanor called Constance to rehearse, standing by the window with her notes. She stumbled twice on the part about ocean air, stopped, and tried again until Constance said it finally made sense. "You persevered," Constance said, "unlike you on Tuesday, when you quit the group project."

"That was different," Eleanor said, but she knew it wasn't, not really. Ms. Menon would like the presentation. Her grandmother would like it even more, telling the story again with the village and the bent backs, and telling it would cost her something each time, the way weather costs the land it feeds.

The kettle ticked as it cooled. Eleanor laid the plate, still clouded with steam, back on the table.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Light slowly fades the dyes and pigments in textiles, paper and some paintings, which is why many museums keep delicate items in dim rooms.
story:
Jeremy had been waiting for the museum field trip for three weeks, mostly because of one room. The poster in Mr. García's classroom showed a quilt sewn in 1852, stitched with red and gold stars, and it was going to be on display for exactly one month before going back into storage. He wanted to see it up close, not in a picture.

On the bus, Susie sat across the aisle from him and Lainey slid into the seat beside him, holding the map of the museum she had printed at home. "Textile gallery is on the second floor," Lainey said, tracing the route with her finger. "Right past the dinosaur hall, so we can look at the T. rex on the way."

Mr. García counted heads at the door, and the class moved through the lobby in a line that kept unraveling. When they reached the textile gallery, Jeremy stopped in surprise. The room was dim, almost shadowy, with small lights aimed low at each case. Susie, walking in behind him, squinted and groaned.

"I can barely see anything in here," she said. "Why would they display the quilt in the dark? That's like hiding it." She leaned toward the case, shading her eyes as if that would help.

Jeremy stood in front of the quilt. The red stars glowed softly, deeper than the poster's bright red, and the gold had gone quiet and honey-colored. He thought about his grandmother's curtains in the front window, how they had bleached pale on the sun side over the years while the side near the wall stayed dark. Same fabric, same dye, different light. He turned to Susie and Lainey.

"I think the dark is on purpose," he said. "Light slowly fades the dyes and pigments in textiles, paper, and some paintings. My grandma's curtains prove it. That's probably why they keep delicate stuff in dim rooms, so the quilt doesn't fade more than it already has." He pointed at a small sign near the case that read "Low light protects fragile fibers."

Susie frowned at the quilt, then at the sign, then at him. "So the dark room isn't a mistake. It's protection." Lainey pulled out her notebook and wrote it down, because she wrote everything down. When a guide walked past, Lainey raised her hand and asked whether the paintings in the big bright gallery down the hall could fade too. The guide said some could, which was why certain canvases there hung behind curtains that were lifted only at certain hours.

Jeremy tested the idea further on the way out. In the lobby, a case of old paper letters sat under a cover, and beside it a case of stone carvings sat under full bright lights, no cover at all. Stone didn't have dye in it the way cloth and paper did. It fit. He told Mr. García, who nodded and said the class vote on lunch had been unanimous for the cafeteria, and that faded dye or not, they still had twenty minutes.

"Wait," Susie said, grabbing his sleeve before they left the gallery. She pulled him back to the quilt case and took one long last look at the red stars glowing in the dimness. "Okay," she said quietly. "Dark room, good idea. I take it back."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it.
story:
The regional spelling bee was held in the public library's meeting room, where shelves of dictionaries formed a wall behind the judges' table. Layla sat in the third row between Raquel and Vince, her word list folded into quarters in her pocket. For two weeks she had reread that list every night, tracing each word with her finger until the pages went soft.

In round four, Raquel got "affluent" and spelled it correctly. In round five, Vince got "obstruct," added an extra "s," and sat down in the audience with his arms crossed. Then the pronouncer said, "Layla. Your word is 'phenomenon.'" Layla opened her mouth and nothing came out. She had read that word at least forty times, but now, standing under the lights, she could not see it on the page in her mind. She spelled it wrong and walked off the stage.

At the refreshment table afterward, Raquel handed her a napkin with a note written on it. "My mom quizzed me out loud every night instead of letting me reread. Want to try it for next year?" Layla read it twice. Raquel had spent less time on her list than Layla had, and she was still in the bee. That did not make sense unless the rereading itself was the problem.

Layla found Mr. Sánchez, the librarian who had organized the event, at the sign-in table. "Raquel's mom quizzed her instead of her rereading. Is that actually better, or did she just get lucky?" Mr. Sánchez pulled a magazine article from his folder. "There's a 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke," he said. "It found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it."

So that was it. Layla had spent hours looking at words and no time at all making herself produce them. She turned the napkin over and wrote her answer on the back: "Yes. Every night. You quiz me Monday, I'll quiz you Tuesday." She handed it to Raquel just as the announcer called the final round, and Raquel stood up, tucked the napkin into her shoe, and walked toward the microphone.

"Affluence," the pronouncer said.

"A-F-F-L-U-E-N-C-E," Raquel said.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
story:
The automatic doors whooshed open, and Grayson walked into the grocery store carrying his mother's list and his last nine dollars from mowing lawns. At the top of the list, in her looping handwriting, was the word strawberries, underlined twice. He pushed the cart toward the produce section and stopped so fast the wheels squeaked. The little sign above the strawberry pint read two dollars. He was almost certain it had read four dollars last month, because four dollars had been the reason he'd gone home empty-handed.

He picked up a pint and turned it in his hands, breathing in that sweet smell that always reminded him of summer. Nearby, a worker in a green apron was stacking crates of berries, crate after crate, until the display looked like a small red hill. Grayson wondered about that. Last month there had been one sad little row of pints. Now there were mountains of them, and they cost half as much. Was that a coincidence, or was there a rule hiding underneath, something he couldn't see directly but could sniff out from clues?

His phone buzzed. It was a text from Ahmad: "did you get the strawberries yet for the smoothie party? my mom says get TWO pints if they're still two dollars." Grayson typed back, "still two. but last month they were four. why would the store make them cheaper when they're this good?" Ahmad replied with three question marks, which was not helpful. Grayson pocketed the phone and decided to run a test, the way Ms. Bighorn had shown them in science class. If berries were cheap because the store suddenly had so many, then other fruits piled up high should also be cheap.

He walked the aisle like a detective. The peaches were stacked three layers deep, and their sign said ninety-nine cents a pound. The blueberries had an entire endcap to themselves and were marked down. Then he reached the grapefruit, sitting alone in a shallow bin, only a few dozen of them, and their price was steep. Pattern confirmed. He felt the idea click into place, like the last piece of a puzzle. It wasn't about the berries being better or worse. It was about how much there was to sell.

"So you figured it out," said a voice. Ms. Bighorn, his neighbor, was standing beside him holding a bag of plums. "Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell." Grayson grinned. "I tested it. Peaches, blueberries, everything that's piled high." Ms. Bighorn laughed and said his method was more sophisticated than most grown-ups managed, and that she'd call it a fair treaty between him and the store: lots of fruit, low price, everyone wins.

At the checkout, Grayson set down two pints of strawberries and tried to justify adding a third, but nine dollars had to cover the milk on the list too. The cashier scanned the berries, and the total came up lower than he'd feared. He slid the pints into his backpack carefully, like treasure.

"Text Ahmad," he told himself, pulling out his phone in the parking lot. "Tell him the treaty holds. Two dollars, two pints, smoothies on."

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Under first-past-the-post, a candidate with 40 votes beats rivals with 35 and 25 votes, even though 60 of the 100 voters chose someone else.
story:
The community centre gym had been desolate all morning, just Alexandre and a folding table, until Shaan burst through the double doors with a cardboard box balanced on one hip. "Ms. Tse says we can use the vote from Saturday's youth council election," Shaan said, setting the box down. "A hundred real ballots. We just can't read the names out loud." Ms. Tse had promised the student council that if they could turn the raw numbers into a presentation for Thursday's open house, she'd let them run the actual voting station next year, the real one, with the real ballot box. That was what Alexandre wanted more than anything, so he had volunteered to be the narrator for the evening, standing at the front with a microphone, walking the audience through the count.

They spread the ballots across two tables. Ophelia made tally marks on a whiteboard while Alexandre sorted, and Shaan transported the piles from table to table in a plastic tub so nothing got mixed. "Pizza Party candidate, forty," Ophelia called out first. "Skate Park candidate, thirty-five. Library candidate, twenty-five." She wrote the numbers big enough to read from the back row, then drew a crown, or something like a crown, over the top one. "Winner, Pizza Party."

"Wait," Alexandre said. He stared at the whiteboard, then at the piles on the table, then at the whiteboard again. The Pizza pile was the biggest, sure. But he put his hands on the other two piles and pushed them together, and the combined stack stood clearly taller than the winner's. He counted to be sure. "Sixty people picked someone else. Sixty out of a hundred. And Pizza still wins." Something about that didn't sit right with him, like a math problem where the answer was correct but the question was wrong.

"So?" Shaan said. "That's how every election works. Most votes wins."

"Most isn't the same as more than half," Alexandre said. He flipped the whiteboard over and drew three long rectangles side by side, divided into ten squares each. He coloured four squares red for Pizza, then three and a half for Skate Park, then the rest for Library, cutting squares in half with the marker until Ophelia complained he was ruining the board. "Look. If the seats were proportional, the red team gets four seats out of ten. The others get six. But the way we did it, red gets everything."

"Proportional," Ophelia repeated, copying the word onto the front of the board where the audience would see it. "Like, the seats match the shares."

They tested it on the ballots themselves. Alexandre dealt them out like cards into ten cups, one cup per imaginary seat, and they watched the piles even out. Then they did it the old way, winner-take-all, and Pizza swept all ten cups. Same hundred ballots, two different results. He wrote both on the board side by side so Thursday's audience would have to look at the gap whether they wanted to or not.

Ms. Tse came by at five o'clock with a box of juice boxes and studied the whiteboard for a long moment. "Good work. Of course, the open house vote on which system to adopt, that'll be run the normal way." She smiled a little as she said it. "One ballot per resident, most votes wins."

Alexandre opened his mouth, then closed it again. He looked at his two rectangles, at his careful proportional seats, at the crown still wobbling over the Pizza Party's forty. "So if forty people want the old way, and sixty split themselves between two kinds of the new way," he said slowly, "the old way wins."

"Exactly," said Ms. Tse, and carried her juice boxes toward the kitchen.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Medicines and cleaning products should be kept up high and out of reach, because young children explore by putting things in their mouths.
story:
Louis had exactly forty-five minutes of babysitting experience, and all of it had happened in the last forty-five minutes, so when two-year-old Penny pointed at the pond and yelled "Duckie!" he decided the park was the greatest idea of his life. The duck was not obstinate, but Penny was. She planted her tiny shoes in the mud by the swings and refused to move until the duck, an ordinary goose, came closer, which it did not, because it had places to be.

"Look, Penny, slide!" Louis said, pointing at the tall blue slide like it was a fireworks show. "Fastest slide in the whole park. Probably the whole city." That worked. She sprinted for the ladder, and Louis followed, texting Derek: babysitting like a pro. Derek texted back a thumbs-up and then, worryingly, a question mark.

While Penny climbed, Ms. Gallagher from across the street settled onto a bench with her coffee and called over, "How's the new job, Louis?" Before he could answer, Penny's mother arrived to take over for the last stretch, and she was carrying the diaper bag, which she set down on the picnic table with a bottle of chewable vitamins sitting in the outer pocket, low and easy to reach. Penny spotted them instantly, of course, because Penny spotted everything instantly. She toddled over and grabbed the bottle and started working the childproof cap with terrifying determination.

Louis's stomach did a slow flip. He remembered his mother dragging a chair to the kitchen counter the day his little cousin learned to crawl, lifting every bottle up high, saying medicines and cleaning products stay up high and out of reach because little kids explore by putting things in their mouths. He had rolled his eyes then. He was not rolling them now. He scooped the vitamin bottle out of Penny's fist, held it high over his head, and Penny stared up at it like he was holding the moon just out of range.

"I want it," Penny announced.

"It's not a snack," Louis said, and placed the bottle on the highest shelf of the little storage box by the picnic tables, way up top where her arms could not dream of reaching. The irony hit him like a dodgeball: he had spent all morning trying to get Penny interested in things, and the one thing she wanted most was the thing he had to keep farthest away. He wrote vitamins, high shelf on the fogged mirror of his brain, and then, because it felt like big news, a real text: Derek. Important. Found out babysitters move stuff up high. Toddlers put EVERYTHING in their mouths. His sister says I should enroll in a babysitting course, and honestly, maybe he would.

"Louis," Penny said, tugging his sleeve with sticky fingers, "duckie came back." The goose was standing three feet away, staring at the sandwich in his pocket.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found.
story:
Sara's wrist still ached from where the model wind turbine had clipped it before the blades flew off the table and shattered the water cup. That part was funny. The part she had typed afterward, in all capitals, about how the school science fair was rigged and everyone knew whose project really should have won, was not. She had deleted it that night, but Amelia had already seen it, and so had half of Mr. Sharma's third period.

"It's gone," Sara said, refreshing her own page for the tenth time. The computer lab smelled like warm dust and lemon cleaner, and the radiator under the window ticked like a slow clock.

Sarina leaned over from the next station, close enough that Sara could hear the keys clicking under her fingers. "Gone where, though? Mr. Sharma said something in media literacy last week. He said the Wayback Machine at the Internet Archive has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found."

"You're making that up."

"Look it up yourself. He put the link on the class page."

Sara's stomach dropped as she typed the address. She had assumed deleting was like erasing a whiteboard, the words gone into nothing. But a page saved somewhere else was more like a photograph of the whiteboard taken before anyone wiped it. She tried her own page first, and the archive offered her a list of dates like rungs on a ladder. She clicked the most recent one.

The page loaded slowly, the fan beside her humming as if the machine were thinking. There it was. Her post, capitals and all, exactly as it had looked before she deleted it, sitting in the archive as calmly as a leaf pressed in a book.

"That's the twist," Sarina said quietly. "You thought deleting was private."

Sara stared at the screen. Public posts, she understood now, lived in a public space, and once something was public it could be copied, quoted, saved. Private spaces were different; her messages to Amelia were not on a public website. The rules were not the rules she had imagined.

"So anyone can still read it," Sara said.

"Anyone who goes looking."

Behind them, a boy was showing his neighbor a project on hereditary traits, and someone at the back could mimic the vice principal's voice so perfectly that half the lab turned around. Sara sat still, one finger resting on the trackpad. Then she opened a new tab and began typing, slowly, a draft of something she might say out loud tomorrow.

"Mr. Sharma's free during lunch," Amelia said.

"I know." Sara read the first line of her draft again, then reached for her backpack. "Let's go find him."

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A "parking lot" is a list where a meeting leader writes down off-topic ideas so they can be discussed later instead of derailing the current item.
story:
Samantha taped the agenda to the kitchen wall and set out four chairs before anyone arrived. The Nature Club had met twice already, and both times the meeting had lasted two hours and decided nothing. Tonight she had three items: the trail cleanup, the poster for the fair, and choosing a club name. She envied her older brother a little; his robotics team always ended on time, and she had never wondered why until now.

Jawad arrived first, then Javier, and finally Ms. Luo from next door, who had offered her living room's folding chairs and stayed to help. Samantha read the first item aloud, and immediately Jawad lit up. "For the cleanup, we should build birdhouses, and also I thought of a way to map the whole wetland, and once we map it we could get a grant." He talked for six straight minutes about grants. The trail cleanup was never mentioned again. When Samantha looked up, twenty minutes were gone, Javier was folding a napkin into a crane, and item one still had no plan attached to it.

She called a break and stood by the sink, thinking. The problem wasn't Jawad's ideas, which were genuinely good. The problem was invisible: something pulled every item sideways, the same way every time. She tested her idea against what she remembered of her brother's meetings. They wrote things down. She remembered the fridge, where her mother kept the agenda from her community group, and there it was in her mother's tidy printing: a box at the bottom of the page labeled Parking Lot, with three stray ideas listed under it. Beneath the box, in smaller letters, her mother had noted "off-topic ideas go here, discuss at the end." Samantha copied the box onto a fresh sheet and carried it back to the table.

She didn't announce a rule. When Jawad began describing a luminous solar lamp he wanted for the birdhouses, she slid the paper toward him and handed him a marker. He wrote "solar lamps," looked at the other two entries already waiting there, and grinned. "Oh, it's like a parking lot. Ideas wait here instead of driving all over the meeting." He capped the marker and turned back to the trails, and the club chose gloves, trash bags, and a Saturday in ten minutes flat.

By the end, the parking lot held five ideas, and they spent the last eight minutes on the two that mattered most. Ms. Luo stood to collect her chairs. "Same time next week?" she asked. "Bring that paper," said Samantha, peeling it off the wall. "It's almost full."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Japan's Obon festival, held in mid-August in most regions and in July in some, honors the spirits of ancestors, who are believed to return home for a visit.
story:
The whole family had crowded into Aunt Hana's house outside Kyoto, and Lillian stood at the edge of it all, holding a paper lantern she was almost afraid to touch. Her grandmother had died in April, and this was the first summer without her. Lillian had texted her friend Maggie before the flight: "I don't even know what you're supposed to do when someone's gone." Maggie had written back, "Maybe that's why your mom's taking you there. To find out."

At dinner, her cousin spread a map on the table and circled their city. "Obon starts here tomorrow," she said, tapping the circle. Lillian frowned, because the calendar in her head said the festival should have been over already. "I thought it was in July," she said. "My friend Larissa read that somewhere." Her cousin shrugged. "In some regions it's held in July. Here it comes in mid-August. Families welcome the spirits of their ancestors home for a visit." The word settled over the table, and everyone nodded like it was the most obvious thing in the world.

Lillian turned that over while she helped wash dishes, her arms aching with the fatigue of the long flight. If Grandma's spirit was coming home for a visit, then "home" mattered. Grandma had lived her whole adult life in Ohio, in a house with a red door and a wind chime that rang even in still air. She had never once been back to Japan after she left. So would she come here, to Aunt Hana's, or would she go looking for a red door on the other side of the world?

Lillian decided to test it. She asked her cousin for a second lantern, and when the family lit theirs and set them along the walkway the next evening, she carried hers to the gate that faced east, toward the ocean, toward home. "In case she comes from that direction," she said. Her cousin studied her for a moment, then set her own lantern beside Lillian's without a word.

Later, when the sky had gone dark and dozens of little flames trembled along the path, Lillian stood at the gate. The breeze shifted, and somewhere behind the house a wind chime she had never noticed before rang twice. It was probably the wind. Probably. But she pulled out her phone and typed to Maggie: "There's a festival here called Obon. I think she found the lantern." She looked up at the small flame steady in the dark, and left the gate open.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: At the equinoxes, around March 20 and September 22, day and night are roughly equal in length all over Earth.
story:
"March twentieth," Vincent muttered, checking his phone for the tenth time. "Today's the day." He stood at the trailhead with Emy-Rose and Melody, waiting for Ms. Balogun to unlock the gate, because tonight he had to explain the seasons to his science class, and his older cousin in Australia had promised a video call at sunset to help him figure something out.

"Explain seasons on a hike?" Emy-Rose said, hoisting her backpack. "The seasons are just... it gets cold, then warm. Done."

"That's a description, not an explanation," Vincent said. "That's the whole category of things I can't do yet." He had a theory, though, and theories could be tested. He'd brought an orange and a marker in his pack, and a question he'd been chewing on for a week: if summer happened because Earth got closer to the sun, then why was his cousin heading into autumn down there at the same moment? He'd tried to petition his mom for an extension on the assignment, and she'd laughed and said no, so the orange was Plan B.

They hiked up through the porous volcanic rock where the trail switchbacked, Ms. Balogun pointing out lichen on the stones. When they stopped for water, Vincent pulled out the orange and jabbed the marker through it at an angle. "Okay, pretend this is Earth. It's tilted. Watch." He spun the orange slowly, tilting the marker's top toward an imaginary sun, then away. "When the top leans toward the sun, summer up here. Six months later the lean goes the other way, and it's summer down there instead. Same distance the whole time. It's the tilt, not how close we are."

Melody grabbed the orange and tried it herself, frowning in concentration. "Wait, but then there'd be a moment right in between. Where neither half is leaning."

"That's what tonight is for!" Vincent's sunset and his cousin's sunset were supposed to match, and if they did, it meant something. He didn't say what yet. He wanted proof first.

At the overlook, the sky burned orange and pink, and right on schedule his phone buzzed. He propped it against a rock, and there was his cousin on the small screen, her own dusk purpling behind her. "Sun's down there," she said. "Sun's down here," Vincent said, and they compared clocks, and the times matched almost to the minute. He threw both fists in the air, startling a bird off the rail. "It's called the equinox," his cousin said, grinning through the static. "Happens again around September twenty-second." Vincent turned to Emy-Rose and Melody, orange held high like a trophy. "Day and night, equal, everywhere on Earth, today. Now watch the tilt do its thing."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: In Excel, a 'bar chart' has horizontal bars and a 'column chart' has vertical bars, although both compare amounts across categories.
story:
Willow had promised herself she would finish Grandpa's watering chart before dinner, and now the laptop screen was laughing at her. Grandpa had kept a notebook all summer, recording how many minutes he watered each corner of his vegetable garden, because the back half near the fence turned arid every July no matter what he did. "Thirty years of squinting at my own handwriting," he had said, sliding the notebook across the kitchen table. "Your mother says you can put it in a spreadsheet. So put it in a spreadsheet."

She typed the numbers into columns, one row for each week, one column for each bed of the garden. Then Ms. Goldberg's voice came back to her from the computer club meeting she had almost skipped. Sum works on a whole column, she had said, and Willow tried it, typing the formula into the cell below the last number. When she pressed Enter, the total appeared like magic: 214 minutes for the tomatoes alone. She sat back, pleased, and thought again about the day she'd decided not to join computer club at all. That had been a mistake, she decided. Probably.

The chart was the next problem. She highlighted the column, clicked Chart, and chose the one labeled bar chart, because that was what she wanted, bars. The chart appeared with the bars lying down flat, sideways, like fence posts after a storm. Willow frowned at it. "That's not right," she said out loud. Grandpa looked over from the sink, drying a plate.

"Your bars fell over," he said.

"Very funny." She stared at the chart, thinking. Maybe the computer hadn't made a mistake. Maybe a bar chart was supposed to look like that, flat, and something else stood up. She scrolled through the chart options and found one called column chart. She clicked it, holding her breath, and the bars rose up straight and tall, each one showing a garden bed, the tomato bar towering over the rest. It compared the amounts exactly the way she needed, just standing instead of lying down. "A bar chart has horizontal bars," she told Grandpa, "and a column chart has vertical bars. I picked the wrong one."

"So which one shows me my garden?"

"The column one. Look, the tomatoes drink twice as much as everything else, and that dry patch by the fence is dead last." Grandpa set down the plate and came to look, one hand on the back of her chair. He tapped the shortest bar with his finger, twice, the way he tapped the notebook when he was thinking.

"That patch," he said slowly, "gets the afternoon sun longest. I always assumed it needed more water, and I've been drowning the poor things at the other end for nothing." He was quiet for a moment, rubbing his jaw. "Thirty years, and it took one chart."

"The spreadsheet did it," Willow said. "I just clicked things."

"You clicked the right things." He pulled out the chair beside her and sat down. "Now, is there a way to make one of these for the thermostat? The tortoise's tank gets cold when she's getting ready to hibernate, and I'd like to see it coming."

Willow grinned and started a new blank sheet. "Grandpa, she's a tortoise, not a mystery. But yes, there's a way."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The King Holiday and Service Act, signed in 1994, made Martin Luther King Jr. Day a national day of volunteer service in the United States.
story:
Hunter had signed up for the food bank shift because Mr. Fortin said the class would volunteer on the school holiday in January, and because Marley had promised there would be doughnuts. There were doughnuts, but they were at the seniors' residence across the parking lot, and the two buildings shared a parking lot, a gravel path, and, apparently, one very confused delivery driver.

"Forty boxes of orange juice," said the driver, stacking crates onto a cart. "Sign here."

"Those are supposed to come to us," Hunter said. "The food bank. The big building with the line of people outside."

"Paperwork says residence." The driver shrugged and drove off before Hunter could argue.

Marley grabbed a crate anyway. "If juice counts as service hours, I'm carrying all forty. I need twelve more hours for the volunteer award, and I am not losing to Clare."

"Clare's ahead of you by three hours and one bake sale," Hunter said. They hauled the crates inside, where the hallway smelled like coffee and a radio was playing quietly. That was when Hunter noticed something odd. The residence was full of people in matching blue T-shirts, folding tables, clipboards. It looked exactly like the food bank set-up across the lot.

He stopped a woman with a clipboard. "Is the residence running a food bank too?"

She laughed. "It's the King Day of Service, honey. Everybody's volunteering today. We've got a whole crew here, and I heard your crew across the lot is short a driver."

Hunter's brain started clicking. His class had the day off school, and Mr. Fortin had called it a service day, but Hunter had never asked why a holiday meant volunteering. On the walk back, Marley's grandmother, who lived in the residence and had come outside in her slippers, settled it.

"You children think you invented being helpful," she said. "The King Holiday and Service Act was signed in 1994. It made Martin Luther King Jr. Day a national day of volunteer service. That's why you're here on your day off instead of sleeping until noon."

"I slept until noon anyway," Marley said. "Then I remembered the hours."

Hunter tested the idea out loud. "So that's why the driver got confused. Two service sites in one parking lot on the one day everybody volunteers. The juice probably belongs to us and the paperwork just went to the wrong door." He checked the labels. Every crate was stamped FOOD BANK in letters nobody could miss, but the delivery slip said residence, one distinct mix-up that explained the whole morning.

They rolled the cart across the lot, and Mr. Fortin raised an eyebrow at it. "Beverage acquisition. Bold strategy."

"Inter-site rescue," Hunter said. "We rescued it. Marley carried thirty-seven of the forty."

"Thirty-eight," said Marley.

Clare appeared with a clipboard of her own. "The driver's coming back for the rest. I called the number on the slip. Also, I'm at fourteen hours."

Marley groaned loudly enough that three people in the food bank line turned around, and Hunter slid the last crate of orange juice onto the stack beside the bread.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
