fact: In the Scripps National Spelling Bee, a speller may start over, but changing any letters already said counts as a misspelling.
story:
Savannah had one goal for the class spelling bee: finally beat Mael, who had won three years running and reminded everyone about it at least once a week. Today he wore his lucky green sweater to Mr. Chatterjee's classroom, as if the sweater could spell for him.

Mr. Chatterjee stood at the whiteboard with his list. "We're using Scripps rules today," he announced. "Study them last night? Good. Hassan, 'monsoon.'"

Hassan got it. Mael got "quarantine." Then Savannah drew "pigeonhole," and her brain did its usual trick of turning to static. "P-I-G..." She stopped. Wrong already. She'd forgotten the silent E? No, wait. P-I-G was fine. It was the end of the word that worried her, the part she hadn't said yet.

She took a breath. "P-I-G-E-O-N-H-O-L-E. Pigeonhole."

"Correct," said Mr. Chatterjee. "Savannah, you started over partway through. That was allowed, but it made me nervous."

"Mr. Chatterjee," Mael said, grinning, "the rule's actually a paradox. Starting over is fine, so it seems like you could fix anything, but the moment you change even one letter you already said, it counts as a misspelling. You can repeat yourself, but you can't undo yourself."

"A paradox in the spelling rules," Hassan said. "That's my kind of bee."

Round after round, kids retired one by one. Bianca retired on "rhubarb" and sat down with theatrical despair. At last it was only Savannah and Mael, and Mr. Chatterjee gave him "eelgrass."

"E-E-L..." Mael paused. His grin flickered. "E-L-G-R-A-S-S."

The room went quiet. Savannah felt her stomach flip. He had changed the second letter, swapped an E for an L after already saying two E's, and everyone in the room knew what that meant. Mr. Chatterjee didn't even need to consult his list.

"That counts as a misspelling," he said gently. "You changed a letter you'd already said. Savannah, if you get this next word, you win."

Savannah suddenly felt less triumphant than she'd imagined. Mael looked like a deflated balloon in his lucky sweater. For three years she'd wanted this exact moment, and now that she had it, she found she wanted a different version of it, one where he messed up an honest impossible word instead of a rule nobody had made explicit enough for him.

"Give him another chance," she said. "Sudden death round."

Mael's head came up. "You're sure? You could just win."

"I've spent a year losing to you. One more word won't kill me."

Mr. Chatterjee raised an eyebrow but reached for the list. "Very well. Mael, 'catastrophe.' And Savannah, I'm noting for the record that you are either very kind or very confident."

"Both," said Hassan from the front row.

Mael spelled "catastrophe" slowly, like a man walking on ice. Then Savannah got "cauliflower" and spelled it without a single pause, without starting over even once, and the classroom erupted.

"Rematch in spring?" Mael said, shaking her hand.

"Bring the sweater," Savannah said. "It clearly needs the exercise."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Research on children at overnight camps has found that most campers feel at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stays mild.
story:
Aurora stood at the trailhead with her pack straps digging into her shoulders and a permission slip folded in her pocket like a secret. In eleven days she would board a bus to Camp Wanata for two weeks, her first time sleeping anywhere but home, and she had spent three nights pretending that thought didn't exist.

Shane scrambled up the first switchback and waited, grinning. "Race you to the creek, unless you're still boycotting cardio because of the mosquito incident."

"That was one time," Aurora said, hiking past him anyway. Tom ambled behind them, nibbling a granola bar, while Mr. Wong, their neighbor who led these Saturday hikes, hummed something off-key at the rear. The trail smelled of pine resin and damp earth, and somewhere below them water knocked against stones.

The problem circled back to her by the second mile, the way it always did. What if she was the only kid at camp who cried into her pillow? She had a plan, though. On Tuesday she had written three questions on an index card, keeping it objective, no feelings involved, just data: do campers miss home, how many, how badly. Tonight she would test one question on Mr. Wong, who had somehow, over four years of hikes, never mentioned a single thing about himself that wasn't about birds.

"Mr. Wong," she called back, "did you ever work at a camp?"

He looked surprised, then said, "I was a counselor for six summers. We asked the kids questions at the start and end, every session."

"What did you find out?"

"That most campers feel at least some homesickness." He shrugged and pointed out a woodpecker, clearly done with the topic. "For most of them it stays mild. That's what the answers said, anyway."

Aurora turned that over for the next half mile, boots crunching gravel, tasting the cold mountain air. Most campers. Most of them, mild. Which meant the kid sobbing in the bunk next to hers, if such a kid existed, might very well be normal. She remembered being seven and refusing a sleepover at Tom's house, then lying awake at midnight listening to her own house settle, wondering if she'd made a mistake. She still hadn't decided. Maybe the sleepover would have gone fine, or maybe she'd have called her mom at 2 a.m. like a defeated general requesting evacuation.

At the creek, Tom skipped stones and Shane waded in up to his ankles, yelping at the temperature. "So," Tom said, casual in a way that was not casual at all, "you're leaving us for camp. Who'll be my hiking mentor now? Mr. Wong teaches me bird calls, but nobody teaches me sarcasm."

"Nobody taught you sarcasm," Aurora said. "It's congenital."

Then Shane sat down hard on a flat rock, and his voice came out smaller than usual. "Can I tell you guys something dumb? I went to overnight camp last summer, and the first three nights I missed my house so much I got a stomachache. I thought I was the only one. Nobody else looked sad."

Tom stopped skipping stones. "I felt homesick at science camp in fifth grade. Whole week."

Aurora laughed, and it came out relieved and strange, echoing off the rocks. "You guys realize we could have shared this information years ago."

Shane wiped his nose on his sleeve and grinned. "Nah. Suffering alone builds character."

At the trailhead that evening, Aurora's mom was waiting by the car with the dog and, Aurora noticed, red-rimmed eyes and a crumpled tissue. "Two weeks is a long time," her mom sniffled. "Are you sure you'll be okay?"

Her mom blew her nose loudly enough to startle a jay out of the tree above them.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: A rainforest climate graph shows a nearly flat temperature line, because temperatures there stay warm and change little from month to month.
story:
Penelope spread the two climate graphs across the picnic table at the campsite, weighting the corners with pinecones so the evening wind could not flip them over. Ms. Ramírez had handed them out before dinner: one for the Sonoran Desert, one for a rainforest in Brazil, each showing monthly rainfall bars and a temperature line. "By tomorrow morning," Ms. Ramírez had said, "tell me which place you'd rather visit, and back it up with the graphs."

Kristian leaned over her shoulder with his flashlight. "Easy. The desert. Look at that rainfall, it barely exists."

"That's not the whole answer," Penelope said. She tapped the desert graph, where the temperature line climbed and dove like a roller coaster across the months. "There it's boiling in some months and cool in others. But this rainforest graph is weird." She ran her finger along the temperature line. It stretched across the page almost flat, like a ruler laid down on the paper.

Kara came back from the washhouse and dropped onto the bench. "Weird how? It's just a line."

"Every month looks the same. That's why I couldn't pick a best month for our trip when my dad asked me last week. I asked the travel agent lady at the mall which month was best, and she just shrugged and said they all look alike." Penelope devised a quick test to make sure she was reading it right. She covered the month labels on the rainforest graph with her bandana, then pointed at random spots along the line. "Kristian, what month is this? This one? This one?" He guessed June, then February, then August, and he was wrong every time, because there was nothing to tell one month from another. On the desert graph, the same game took him two seconds.

"So if we go to the rainforest," Kara said slowly, "we don't have to worry about picking the wrong month for the weather? It's warm the whole year?"

"That's what the graph says. Temperatures there stay warm and barely change from month to month, so the line sits flat." Penelope wrote that in her notebook, then compared it against the desert graph, where a traveler really could pick a good month or a terrible one. She flipped the page over and drew a wobbly line and a flat one side by side, labeling them like a poster. "Maybe I'll be the graph ambassador tomorrow. Convincing people with flat lines instead of arguments."

"That's not even a real job," Kristian said, but he was grinning.

"It's plausible," Penelope said, and capped her pen.

Ms. Ramírez walked past with the coffee pot and glanced at the table. "Find something interesting?"

Penelope held up the rainforest graph, bandana still covering the months. "Pick a month," she said. "Any month. I dare you."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, shiva, from the Hebrew word for 'seven', is a seven-day period of mourning after a burial, when visitors come to comfort the family.
story:
Aiden stood on his aunt's porch holding a plate of cookies his mother had sent, and he could not remember a single thing he had planned to say. Inside, his grandfather's shiva had been going for three days already, and Aiden had spent all three of them in the kitchen refilling juice pitchers so he would not have to walk into the living room where everyone sat on low chairs, talking about Zayde.

Laith had come with him after school, mostly because Aiden had begged him to. "So we just go in?" Laith whispered, peeling off his backpack. "What do I say to your grandma?"

"That's the problem," Aiden said. "I don't know. I figured there was some script, like a thing you're supposed to say, and nobody gave me the copy." He had presumed the grown-ups all knew the words and were waiting for him to learn them too, like a secret handshake he'd missed.

Inside, the living room was warm and smelled of coffee. Every chair was full, and the ones Grandma and his aunts sat on were cushions set close to the floor. Mr. Goh, from next door, was perched awkwardly on a piano bench with a paper cup, nodding along while an aunt told a long story about Zayde's terrible parallel parking. Aiden realized he was still holding the cookies like a shield.

He tested his theory quietly, by watching. When Talia from his Hebrew school class arrived, she walked straight to Grandma, said the Hebrew words for "may you be comforted," and then just sat down next to her. She didn't say anything wise. She didn't say anything at all for a while. And Grandma leaned slightly toward her, like a plant toward a luminous window, and kept talking about parking.

Aiden put the cookies on the table and sat on the rug beside his aunt. "Tell the one about the fishing rod," he said. She did, and it was even worse than he remembered, and everyone laughed anyway, even Grandma, who laughed like it surprised her.

Later, in the kitchen, Laith stacked cups. "So the seven days," he said. "Somebody told me shiva means seven. You just let people come be with you the whole time?"

"Seven days, and yeah," Aiden said. "The whole point is showing up. Nobody cares about the words." He rinsed a cup and considered this like a math problem where the variable he'd been solving for turned out not to matter. Three days he'd spent hiding in the kitchen, and the answer had been the sitting.

There were four days left. On the fifth, he planned to bring his chemistry cards and quiz Talia by the low chairs, because Zayde had loved chemistry and had cheated at it shamelessly. For now he carried a fresh pot of coffee into the living room, set it down next to Mr. Goh, and took the empty spot on the rug.

"Alright," he said. "Tell it again. The parking one."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Brackets are cleared with the distributive property before solving: 3(x + 2) becomes 3x + 6, because the 3 multiplies both terms inside.
story:
The whiteboard at the front of Room 12 said "MATH CLUB" in Ms. Friedman's green marker, and underneath it, the problem of the week: 3(x + 2) = 18. Kaitlyn copied it into her notebook and stared at it while the other kids found seats.

"Twenty minutes," said Ms. Friedman, checking the clock. "First correct answer with a check gets to pick the puzzle for next week." She sat down at her desk and graded quizzes, because the rule of math club was that nobody got fed an answer, not even by a teacher.

Kaitlyn wanted the puzzle pick. She had been first twice this year, and the folder of brainteasers Jayde had brought from her grandmother, old logic games from her family's heritage, was still sitting unopened on the shelf because nobody had chosen it yet.

She started the way she always did. Get x alone. She wrote 3x + 2 = 18, subtracted 2 from both sides, and got 3x = 16, so x = 16/3. She frowned. The answer to a club problem was almost never a fraction like that, but the board was stubborn and her arithmetic looked clean, so she checked it anyway. She put 16/3 back into the original equation, multiplied, and the two sides came out different. Not close. Different.

"You look mad," said Anne from the next desk, leaning over.

"It won't check. Watch." Kaitlyn substituted her answer out loud. "Three times 16/3 is 16, plus 2, that's 18 on the left. But the right side is already 18, so I'd need the bracket part to be 6, not 18." She stopped. She read her first line again. "Anne, I only multiplied the x. The 3 has to hit the 2 also."

"So what does it actually become?"

"3x + 6," Kaitlyn said. "Because the 3 multiplies both terms inside." She crossed out her old work, feeling her face go warm, since she had explained brackets to Jayde just last week and now the mistake embarrassed her. She rewrote it: 3x + 6 = 18. Subtract 6 from both sides, 3x = 12. Divide both sides by 3. x = 4. She checked it fast, substituting 4 into the original: 4 plus 2 is 6, and 3 times 6 is 18. Both sides matched.

Her hand went up before she could talk herself out of it. "Ms. Friedman, x equals 4."

Ms. Friedman walked over, read the check line, and tapped the page once. "Show Jayde the bracket step before you pick your puzzle."

Kaitlyn carried her notebook to the shelf, set it down beside the folder, and opened the cover to the first page.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In German, a customer can ask for the bill by saying "Die Rechnung, bitte," meaning "The bill, please."
story:
Every Saturday, Aurora's grandmother turned her kitchen into a café, and Aurora was the only customer. "Guten Tag," Grandmother would call, tying on an apron, and Aurora had to answer in German or go hungry, at least in theory. Today Aurora had brought backup: Jawad and Kamden, who had heard about the free cake and refused to stay home.

"We're going to simulate a real restaurant," Aurora told them, dragging the small table to the middle of the kitchen so it sat diagonal to the counter, the way tables in her grandmother's old photographs stood. "Grandma waits tables, we order. But everything has to be in German, or she won't bring anything."

"That's a trap," Kamden said, but he sat down anyway.

Aurora went first, since she had practiced. "Ich möchte ein Stück Kuchen," she said, slowly, and Grandmother beamed and swept off toward the counter. Jawad tried next, mangling the word for cake so badly that Kamden laughed into his sleeve, but Grandmother brought him a slice anyway and said, "Good try," which Aurora suspected was against the rules. Kamden pointed at the cake and said "Kuchen" and got two slices, which seemed like a reward for cheating.

Then came the part Aurora had been dreading. Cake was not free forever; at some point the meal ended, and she did not know how to make it end. She waved at Grandmother, who only waved back. She tried "Danke," and Grandmother smiled and kept polishing the counter. Her reasoning went like this: in a restaurant you could not just leave, and you could not grab the bill yourself, so there had to be a sentence that summoned it, the same way "Ich möchte" summoned cake. She had heard Grandfather say something at the end of dinner last week, something with a b sound at the end.

"Die Rechnung, bitte," Aurora tried.

Grandmother set down her cloth and came over so fast that Kamden sat up straight. A slip of paper appeared on the table, a real one, with numbers written in Grandfather's looping hand.

"What did you say?" Jawad whispered.

"Die Rechnung, bitte," Aurora whispered back. "It means the bill, please."

Kamden read the paper and groaned. "Five euros for cake? We're paying in pretend money, right?"

Grandmother stood at the counter, not moving, watching the slip of paper in the middle of the table. Aurora noticed then that Grandmother's eyes were shining and that she was holding the edge of the counter with both hands, the way she held the railing on the porch steps. Grandfather came in from the garden, saw the little table and the paper, and put his hand briefly on Grandmother's shoulder before he sat down at the diagonal table with them.

"Another week of practice," Grandmother said, "and I will bring the coffee, too."

"Three Kaffee," Grandfather ordered, "and one for the waitress, when she is finished."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The word "propaganda" comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622.
story:
Mathis had seventy-two dollars saved, and the sneakers on his screen cost sixty-nine, which left almost nothing for tax. The ad showed a basketball player he actually recognized, midair, with the words "Everyone's Already Switching" printed in gold across the bottom. He turned his desk chair toward the window, where the neighbor's cat was watching a rodent hole under the fence with total patience, then turned back to the screen. It was just a shoe. He knew that. But the player wore them, and everyone had switched, apparently, and the timer in the corner said the sale ended in nine minutes.

His phone buzzed. Graysen had sent the same ad with the message "GET THESE." Mathis typed back, "You buying them?" and Graysen answered with a single thumbs-up. Lennox sent a message two seconds later: "Don't. My cousin got them and the sole peeled in a week." Mathis stared at the two replies side by side, like the phone itself was arguing.

He opened a new tab instead of the checkout page, because Mr. Carvalho's vocabulary assignment was still due Monday and the word he'd pulled was "propaganda." He'd figured it was a war word, something governments invented. The etymology site said otherwise. "From the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide," he read aloud, "a Catholic Church committee set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622." A committee for spreading the faith. He sat with that for a second. So the word didn't start with dictators at all; it started with a group whose whole job was persuasion, and the name just stuck to everything that came after. "Huh," he said to the empty room.

He went back to the ad tab and looked at it again, deliberately, like Mr. Carvalho had taught them to look at poems. "Everyone's Already Switching" was a bandwagon appeal, making him feel like the only kid on earth still in his old shoes. "Game-changing" and "weak" for every other brand were loaded words, doing the work that facts were supposed to do. And the player was a testimonial, a famous face standing in for proof. Three tricks, all pointed at his seventy-two dollars.

He tried something. He closed the tab, waited, and searched the shoe name followed by the word "review." The forum threads were long and plain, and Lennox's cousin was not alone. One guy said his pair survived a whole season; three others mentioned the sole. It wasn't a pattern yet, but it leaned one direction, and hereditary loyalty to a brand, which Mathis realized he'd kind of inherited from his dad, wasn't a good enough reason to ignore it.

The countdown would have expired by now. He texted Graysen, "Maybe hold off, check reviews first," and got back a shrug emoji, which meant no. Mathis closed his laptop and went downstairs, where his dad was at the kitchen table, holding a newspaper advertisement for a blender endorsed by a TV chef, turning it over to look at the coupons on the back. "Thinking about it," his dad said. "Everyone's buying these now." Mathis pulled out a chair.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: Spanish speakers ordering politely often say "Quisiera...", a softer form of "querer" (to want) that means "I would like..."
story:
Anthony raised his hand halfway, then let it drop. Mr. Kaya had turned the language classroom into a restaurant again, with the desks pushed together and paper menus spread across them, and Anthony still could not make himself say the sentence out loud. He wanted to order lunch in Spanish without freezing, and tomorrow his class was walking to the real place on Miller Street, where the owner actually spoke Spanish.

Theo leaned over from the next table. "Just say quiero. Quiero un taco. Done." He said it loudly, grinning, because Theo was immune to embarrassment in a way Anthony had never managed.

Anthony tried it. "Quiero un taco, por favor," he said to Laurianne, who was playing the server, and she wrote it down without looking up. But something bothered him. The weekend before, at the taqueria with his uncle, Anthony had watched a man at the counter say quiero this and quiero that, and the woman behind the register had answered him in flat, tired English. Two customers later, someone ordered in a softer, longer word, and the woman's whole face changed. She smiled. She added extra salsa. Anthony had been too nervous to catch the word at the time, but he remembered the sound of it: kis-air-ah.

He turned his menu over and looked at the vocabulary list in the margin. Quisiera. There it was, printed small. "Quisiera un taco," he said to Laurianne, watching her face.

She looked up this time. Her expression did the same thing the taqueria woman's had. "Ah, mejor," she said, and then, in English, almost to herself, "Quisiera means 'I would like.' It's a softer way of saying quiero." She set down her pencil like a real server would. "How much is it, then? Ask me."

"¿Cuánto cuesta?" Anthony asked, and when she told him, he counted out the play money without fumbling.

At lunch, Anthony weighed whether to tell Theo he had been wrong, or whether that was a compromise Theo would not accept. There was a motive behind Theo's loudness, Anthony thought, the same motive behind his own silence: nobody wanted to look like the beginner. On the walk home, Theo kicked a bottle cap the whole length of the block.

At the restaurant on Miller Street, the owner took Theo's order first. Theo said quiero. Then it was Anthony's turn, and he felt the old fear rise, and said it anyway. "Quisiera el pollo con arroz, por favor. ¿Cuánto cuesta?"

The owner smiled the way Laurianne had, the way the woman at the taqueria had, and reached for the good plate behind the counter.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The First Amendment to the US Constitution protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly and petitioning the government.
story:
Mya had the pocket Constitution rolled in her fist like a baton, and she unrolled it for the tenth time under the fluorescent lights of the town hall basement. The room smelled of burnt coffee and damp umbrellas, and the folding chairs were already filling up because tonight the council would vote on whether to cut the budget for the wildlife preserve, where the bison and the elk lived. "Herbivores," Johan whispered, pointing at a photo taped to the petition table. "Every animal on that preserve is a herbivore. No predators, just grass eaters." Zane nudged Mya. "You're up after the drainage guy. Still going to say your part?"

Mya nodded, though her mouth had gone dry. She had signed up to speak because a rumor was going around school, a rumor that sounded almost sinister: that the town planned to ban a student group from printing its newspaper in the library basement, just because the paper had criticized the drainage project. Nobody could prove it, so Mya had decided to find out what actually protected the paper. She had asked the librarian, then a cousin, and finally she had sat at her kitchen table with the little booklet until she could say it without looking.

The drainage guy talked about pipes for eleven minutes. Then the clerk called, "Mya Okafor, three minutes," and Mya walked to the mic on legs that felt like water.

"I'm here about the student newspaper," she said. Her voice wobbled, then steadied. "Some of us heard the town might stop us from printing it. I wanted to know what protects us, so I looked it up. The First Amendment to the US Constitution protects freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government." She paused, took a breath, and gave it in her own words, the way she had practiced in the mirror. "What that means to me is that we can believe what we believe, say what we think, print what we write, stand together peacefully, and bring our complaints right here, to this room, to you."

Ms. Nwosu, who ran the preserve booth by the door, started clapping first, and then the whole back row joined in. One council member leaned into her microphone. "Can you cite where it says that, young lady?"

"Amendment One," Mya said. "First on the list."

"First," the council member repeated, and made a note on her pad. "For the record, no one is banning any newspaper in this town. But I like hearing a citizen who does her homework before she panics."

Afterward, Zane bought her a hot chocolate from the machine by the restrooms, and it tasted like powdered marshmallows and victory. Johan was already sketching a headline on a napkin: LOCAL HERD OF HERBIVORES SAVED, STUDENT PRESS SAFE. "You're going to write the real story, right?" he said. Mya pulled the pen from his hand and printed her name at the top of the napkin, right under the headline. "Editor," she said. "It goes right there."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In American English, a comma or period that ends a quotation goes inside the closing quotation marks; British usage often places it outside.
story:
Cooper sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with three crumpled drafts of his story for Ms. Chan's assignment spread in front of him. The story was about a boy who finds a venomous snake in the woodshed and has to decide whether to run or warn his little brother. The problem was the dialogue. Every time he wrote a line of speech, he felt like he was guessing where the commas belonged, and guessing was not going to get him a climax that Ms. Chan called "clear and earned."

"There's an old typewriter in the attic," his grandfather said, carrying two mugs of cocoa. "If you're going to suffer over punctuation, you might as well do it with a machine that suffers too."

Cooper laughed, but he climbed the attic stairs anyway, because Freyja had promised to email him her story that afternoon. Freyja was spending the semester in England with her aunt, and she and Cooper had agreed to swap drafts and mark each other's dialogue, since Ms. Chan had said the best way to learn punctuation was to hunt for it in someone else's page.

Her story arrived while he was still in the attic, dust on his knees, a startled rodent skittering out from behind the typewriter case. He read her story on his phone: a girl who thrives on dares until one goes badly wrong on a frozen lake, with a climax right where a climax should be. Then he looked at her comments on his story, and his stomach dropped. She had circled every comma and period that ended a quotation and drawn arrows pointing outside his closing quotation marks. "Wrong," she had written beside one, "should be after the marks."

Cooper stared at the arrows. Was she teasing him? He pulled up the rule sheet Ms. Chan had given the class and read it twice. In American English, a comma or period that ends a quotation goes inside the closing quotation marks. His version was right, wasn't it? He checked Freyja's own story, and there it was, plain as the attic dust: she had put her commas and periods outside the quotation marks, every single time. So either Freyja was wrong about everything, or something stranger was going on. He typed a reply: "Why did you move my commas out and then put yours out too?"

While he waited, he drafted his snake story again on paper, moving a comma inside the marks, then outside, then inside, watching the sentence change shape on the page. His grandfather appeared in the attic doorway with a folder of old letters under his arm.

"Letters from a friend in Manchester, from when I was about your age," his grandfather said, tapping the folder. "You're not the first person in this family to argue with England about punctuation. I never did settle it, you know. I'd like to, someday."

Cooper's phone buzzed. "We do it differently here," Freyja had written. "British usage often puts it outside the marks. Ask your grandfather, then tell me who wins."

Cooper looked from the phone to the folder, wondering where a sixty-year-old argument about commas had been hiding all this time. "Grandpa," he said, "how do you feel about a rematch?"

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Thin paper buckles, or cockles, when soaked with washes, so watercolour artists often use heavy paper of about 300 grams per square metre, also sold as 140-pound paper.
story:
Lillian had until Friday to finish a watercolour portrait of her grandmother for the school art show, and so far she had three failed attempts drying on the windowsill. Each one had the same flaw: the face looked flat, and the paper itself had buckled into soft waves that caught the light like a lake.

"Mine did that too," Alexis said, holding up her portrait of her dog. The paper had rippled so badly that the dog's nose sat on a ridge. "Ms. Abdi said we're supposed to build the face with washes, light ones first, then darker ones on top. But every time I add a layer, it gets wavier."

Lillian looked at her own attempts. The printer paper she had taken from the classroom tray was thin, and she began to suspect that the waves were not caused by her brushwork at all. Alexis layered carefully and still got waves. Brynlee, who had painted almost nothing, also had waves. The pattern pointed at the paper, not the painters.

She found Ms. Abdi after last period. "Could I test something? Could I paint the same wash on two different papers and see which one buckles?"

Ms. Abdi opened the cabinet and handed her a thick pad. "This is what watercolour artists often use. It's 300 grams per square metre, also sold as 140-pound paper. Try your experiment."

Lillian recruited Brynlee to hold the sheets flat while she brushed an identical pale wash across the printer paper and across the heavy pad. By the time the bell rang, the thin sheet had risen into ridges that Brynlee recognized at once. "It's cockling," Brynlee said. "That's what the buckling is called." The heavy sheet lay flat, its surface still smooth.

On Thursday evening Lillian started the portrait again on a sheet cut from the pad. She laid the palest wash first, waited for it to dry, then added the shadow under her grandmother's cheekbone, then the crease at her eye. Four layers, each darker than the last, and the paper stayed flat the whole time. The face came forward out of the page instead of sitting on top of it.

Friday morning she carried the portrait to the gym, where Ms. Abdi was taping names beside the display boards. Brynlee and Alexis were already there. "Your grandmother looks like she's about to say something," Alexis said. Lillian propped the painting on the easel and stepped back. From across the gym, the flat paper caught the light evenly, and her grandmother looked out at her, mid-sentence.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Shirley Jackson's story The Lottery, published in The New Yorker in 1948, opens with children piling up stones, a detail that hints at how the lottery ends.
story:
Mr. Rao handed back the copies of The Lottery on Tuesday and told the class to turn to the first paragraph again. Hunter had read the story the night before, and the ending had kept him awake for an hour, so he was ready to argue about it.

"Nobody told us what the prize would be," said Caylee, tapping her paper. "That's cheating. You can't just spring that on a reader."

"You can," said Mr. Rao. "But you can't spring it with no warning at all. Reread the opening. Tell me what you find."

Hunter looked down at the paragraph. It described a clear morning, flowers, green grass, and boys gathering stones into piles while the girls watched. That was all. He had skimmed it the first time because it seemed like nothing, the kind of opening where nothing happens. Now he read it slowly.

"Wait," he said. "The stones."

"What about them?" said Mr. Rao.

"They're collecting them. Like it's a game." Hunter kept staring. "But at the end, that's what they use. Nobody has to run and find rocks. They already made the piles." He sat back. "So the writer put it right there, in the first paragraph, and I skipped it."

"Then you can infer the ending before it happens," Mr. Rao said. "If you pay attention. Jackson published that story in The New Yorker in 1948, and people wrote angry letters because they felt tricked. But the trick was fair. The clue was on page one."

Caylee frowned at her paper. "So the stones are a symbol too? Like they stand for the whole town?"

"That's yours to argue on Friday," said Mr. Rao. "One page. Evidence from the text." The bell rang, and he added over the noise, "The fall festival bake sale revenue pays for these class sets of books, so thank the bake sale committee."

Hunter walked out with Maxwell, who had been quiet the whole period. "I put those stones on your desk," Maxwell said.

"What stones?"

"Before class. You didn't notice? Left corner, three little pebbles in a pile. I did it while you were getting water."

Hunter stopped in the hallway. He thought back. When he had sat down, he had swept his hand across the corner of the desk out of habit, and three small pebbles had clattered to the floor. He hadn't looked at them. He had been thinking about the bake sale list on his phone, because his mother had signed up to make two dozen muffins.

"Before we even discussed it," Hunter said. "So the ending was sitting on my desk the whole time, and I brushed it off."

Maxwell grinned. "One page for Friday, remember. Write about the pebbles."

"That's not in the text."

"Make it a preface. Mr. Rao likes a hook." Maxwell headed for the stairs. "And don't sweep your desk tomorrow. I'm doing four this time."

Hunter opened his binder on the bench outside the gym and began to write, one line under the next, his handwriting sparse at first and then filling the page fast.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: To test whether n is prime, you only need to try divisors up to its square root, because if n is a times b, one of them is no bigger than that root.
story:
Naomi typed her prime checker for the third time and ran it on the number 999,983. The cursor blinked in the console and nothing happened. "It's frozen," she said. Linden leaned over from the next computer, chewing the end of his stylus. "Mine froze too. Ms. Santoso said try smaller numbers." Naomi tried 97, and the answer printed instantly. Then she tried 9,991. Instant. Then 99,991. The program hung again, spinning through divisor after divisor in its loop.

"It's not frozen," Maddison said from across the room. "It's just slow. My brother says big checks take longer." Naomi stared at the screen. She had written the loop herself, in the coding club room with its posters about women in computer science and its smell of dry-erase markers. Her program asked for a number, then tried dividing it by 2, then 3, then 4, all the way up. For 9,991 that was nearly ten thousand divisions. For 99,991, nearly a hundred thousand. The waiting wasn't random, she realized. It was proportional. Double the number, and the loop did about twice the work.

She grabbed a scrap paper. The club was supposed to end in twenty minutes, and the showcase was next week, where their programs would precede the awards in the auditorium. She couldn't stand at the front with something that froze. She wrote 9,991 equals 99 times 101. Then 999,983 and, after some stabbing at her calculator, 999,983 equals 757 times 1,321. She looked at the two factor pairs. In the first pair, 99 was smaller. In the second pair, 757 was smaller. She tried another, 143 equals 11 times 13. Again, one factor was small and one was large.

"To test whether a number is prime, you only need divisors up to its square root," she said slowly, reading the idea off her own scribbles. "Because if n is a times b, one of them is no bigger than that root." Linden frowned. "So if nothing divides it by the square root, nothing ever will." Naomi changed one line in her loop, capping the divisor at the square root of n, and ran 999,983 again. NOT PRIME, printed before she could even tap her foot.

Maddison came over and typed 1,000,003, a number Naomi had never dared to try. The answer snapped onto the screen in under a second. "Okay, that's the frontier broken," Maddison said, and Naomi laughed, because it felt exactly like that, like the slow old edge of her program had been pushed back to somewhere far away. She saved the file and started a new one at the top of the screen: PRIME CHECKER, VERSION 2.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Glasses for astigmatism use cylindrical lenses, which bend light more in one direction than in the other.
story:
Ella had squinted at the whiteboard for two months before her mother finally booked the appointment, so she walked into the eyeglasses store expecting the worst. Leyla came along because she had nothing better to do, and because she said watching Ella pick frames would be better than television.

"You're overthinking it," Leyla said, spinning the frame rack so the options circulated past them like a slow carousel.

Ella chose plain black frames, mostly to be done with choosing. But when Mr. Oyelaran, the optician, slid the new lenses into the frame, he said something that snagged in her mind. "You have astigmatism, so these are cylindrical lenses. They bend light more in one direction than in the other."

More one way than the other. Ella turned that over while Mr. Oyelaran adjusted the nose pads. It meant the lens was not like a magnifying glass, which stretched everything evenly. It had a direction, like wood grain. If that was true, then turning the lens should turn the stretch with it. She lifted the glasses off before he could stop her, held one lens up at the store's front window, and rotated the frame slowly sideways.

The street outside warped. The awning across the road, wide as a canopy, squeezed narrow, then stretched tall, then squeezed again as she turned. The lamp post thinned and fattened. Leyla leaned in and tried it herself, and the shop became a funhouse mirror in her hand.

"You're going to bend something," Mr. Oyelaran said, but he was almost smiling. "You found the axis. That's the whole trick of the lens."

Ella put the glasses on properly and the world snapped into focus. Signs across the street had letters with actual edges. She could read the bus schedule taped inside the shelter, could even count the pigeons on the wire, which before had been a single gray smudge. She had spent a term being negligent about it, copying Leyla's notes instead of looking at the board, and now the problem had a shape. A stretched, tilted, fixable shape.

"So I can see everything now," Ella said, stepping out onto the sidewalk.

"Everything," Leyla agreed.

Ella turned her head to admire the street, and the whole world tipped and swam, because with new lenses, moving your eyes the old way takes practice too. She grabbed the lamppost, blinked twice, and laughed.

"Okay," she said. "Tomorrow, the whiteboard."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A primary source is a firsthand record from the time, such as a letter, photograph or official data, and it is often the best place to check a claim.
story:
The message from Colt popped up at 9:47 on a Tuesday night: "Someone on the town history page says the mill burned down in 1893 and that's why the founders left. Mr. Russo replied 'interesting claim' with a wink emoji. Is he making fun of the guy?"

Jake leaned closer to the screen. The town history page had forty replies under it, half of them arguing. The mill fire was controversial, apparently, because the other half of the replies insisted the founders left after a flood, and someone had called someone else a liar in all caps. Jake's mom shouted from the kitchen that if he wanted the truth he should stop reading comment sections, but the comment section was exactly where the fight was.

"Who's right?" Colt typed.

Instead of answering, Jake tried to formulate a search that would settle it. Not a search for opinions, though. He typed "Bramble Creek newspaper archive" and found that the library had scanned every issue of the Bramble Creek Courier onto a website, all the way back to the 1880s. A note on the front page read: "A primary source is a firsthand record from the time, such as a letter, photograph or official data." He read the line twice.

"So it's not somebody's opinion about what happened," Jake said out loud to the empty room. "It's the thing that was there when it happened." He typed into the chat: "A primary source. A letter or a photo or official data from the time itself. Better than a comment from a guy named MillDude88."

He started with June 1893 and paged forward. The Courier was glorious trash. There was an advertisement for Dr. Priddy's Tonic, guaranteed to purge the intestine of every impurity known to science. There was a photograph of the new bridge with half the town standing on it in stiff collars. There was a letter to the editor complaining about hogs on Main Street. Then, on page one of July 11, 1893, a headline in enormous type: MILL DESTROYED BY FIRE.

"There it is," Jake said. "The fire's real."

But below the headline, the story said the mill's owners had already announced they were leaving for Denver, and that the fire had broken out three weeks after the announcement. So the fire couldn't be why the founders left. Jake scrolled back through June, looking for the reason, and found a short item about a flood that spring that had ruined the waterwheel. Both sides of the comment war had been holding a real piece of the story and calling the other side liars.

"Screenshot it," Colt typed. "Post it before MillDude88 wakes up."

Jake's cursor hovered over the reply button. Forty people were still arguing down there, and none of them had opened the archive. He pasted the link, typed "read the July 11, 1893 issue yourself," and stopped, thumb resting on the enter key.
